newsitem.title: USA: Academics see scope for further U.S. rate hikes.
newsitem.headline: Academics see scope for further U.S. rate hikes.

text.p: U.S. academics said robust growth and high levels of resources utilization, mainly labor, would likely lead the Federal Reserve to raise short-term interest rates again, possibly as early as July.

"It's likely there will be another rate increase before the end of the summer. Whether there'll be another one after that will depend on what happens between now and late summer," John Taylor, professor of economics at Stanford University, told Reuters.

The Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) left short-term interest rates unchanged when it met last week. In March, the FOMC hiked the federal funds rate by 25 basis points to 5.50 percent, a move Fed Chairman Alan Greenspan described as "a form of insurance" against inflation risk.

"The attempt to raise interest rates in anticipation of inflation is what is being considered (by the Fed) right now. That's being preemptive," Taylor said. "The question is whether it (Fed policy) is preemptive enough or not."
Taylor described the Fed's inaction last week as "basically a delay, not a decision not to tighten."

Taylor tied his forecast to concern that "inflation will pick up toward the end of the year," adding that at least one rate hike was likely "unless there is a slowdown and an actual reduction in the rate of inflation," though there is "no evidence for that yet."
"You can't base monetary policy on hope. It's a judgment call here. They may very well turn out to have been late," Taylor said.
Former Fed Vice Chairman Alan Blinder said the Fed's inaction in May did not mean the end of preemptive policy.

"Suppose that, in July, the unemployment rate remains at around 5.0 percent, inflation indices start to point up. The Fed can raise interest rates by 50 basis points," said Blinder. "It would still be preemptive."

Blinder, now a professor of economics at Princeton University, said he would have favored a 50-basis-point hike in March or a second move in May due to the risk associated with rapid growth and low unemployment.
"The real way a central bank gets credibility is by matching its deeds to its words. It's almost the dictionary definition of credibility," Blinder noted.
Laurence Ball, Professor of Economics at Johns Hopkins University, agreed "the best forecast for whether inflation is going to rise is real growth and unemployment."

"There is some risk policy is too easy and the Fed will come around this and raise rates," said Ball, while cautioning the Fed's inaction may indicate "rates will remain fairly steady through the end of the year."
Ball said the Fed showed a willingness to take risk.
"It's conceivable the NAIRU (Non-Accelerating Inflation Rate of Unemployment) has come down to 5.0 percent, but it's a gamble to assume that has happened," Ball noted.

"The idea there is a brave new world out there with lower unemployment, higher growth and no inflation is highly speculative at best," said Ball, who described himself as "dovish" on inflation. "Greenspan's actions never matched his rhetoric. If he had literally followed his rhetoric, he would have tightened."
Gregory Mankiw, professor of economics at Harvard University, said the Fed's inaction last week showed central bankers are circumspect because they are sailing "uncharted waters."

"The Fed has to worry about two problems: inflation and unemployment," Mankiw said. "Obviously, the Fed has neither problem right now. The problem is which of the two does Greenspan need to worry the most about right now."
Mankiw acknowledged the Fed is coming under political pressure -- though not from the White House.
"I don't think that motivated Greenspan's decision (last week)," said Mankiw who added "the Fed does not want to put us in the situation of Japan where you have deflation."
